name: Erik Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Dennis Hale's garage on Mill Road, three bays, and I've been there since I was sixteen as an apprentice. Most of what comes in is farm pickups, older diesels and the yearly safety inspections, plus whatever the locals break on a Saturday. I like a job where you can hear what's wrong before you open the bonnet.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The newer cars, if I'm honest, where you can't change a bulb without plugging in a computer. Dennis bought a diagnostic tablet with an AI helper on it last year, and I leave that to Josh, our apprentice. I'd rather use my ears and a good torch.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Chiara, she's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we're getting married next September at St Anne's. We bought a little terraced house two years back, my dad helped with the deposit, and I've got about ten months of wages put by. I don't spend much, never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how I'd like it to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, loudly, probably at the pub after Thursday football. People have been saying computers would replace mechanics since my granddad's day. Cars still break and someone still has to get under them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, that's what I actually expect anyway. My work's steady, Dennis has more jobs than bays, and there are three other garages in town that would take me tomorrow. The only thing that bothers me is the carmakers locking up their software, and that's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd carry on at Dennis's, keep putting money aside for the wedding, and pay a chunk off the mortgage early. I might finally do the air conditioning certificate Dennis keeps on about, because that's real work people pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. That's the world I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said carmakers locking up their software bothers you. How does that show up in your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a farmer brought in a two-year-old pickup with a warning light, and we couldn't clear it without paying the maker for a software key. That's forty minutes and a fee for something I could fix with a spanner. That's what's killing small garages, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your job that the AI tools in this picture would touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bookings and the invoices, maybe, but Dennis's wife Carol does those and she's quicker than any computer. And the tablet Josh uses, I suppose. I'd let him keep it.

say: He'd say **told you so** loudly at the pub.
Cars still break, and someone still has to **get under them**.
think: This is the world he **actually expects**, with steady work and garages hiring.
His real gripe is carmakers **locking software**, which has nothing to do with AI.
do: Carry on at **Dennis Hale's garage** with no changes.
Save for the **wedding** and pay a chunk off the **mortgage** early.
feel: **Calm** and settled, because this is the world he'd choose.
S0.quote: People have been saying computers would replace mechanics since my granddad's day. Cars still break and someone still has to get under them.
fieldNote: His trust is in **ears, torch and spanner**, not the diagnostic tablet.
He blames **carmakers' software locks**, not AI, for squeezing small garages.
He hands screen work to Josh, the apprentice, and to Carol, the owner's wife who does **the books**.

steps.text: Keep fixing farm pickups and diesels at Dennis Hale's garage
Pay a lump off the mortgage and save for the September wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's more like what the papers keep saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says, that a trade is a trade and you can't download a mechanic. At work I'd tell Josh to stop staring at that tablet and learn to listen to an engine. Online I don't post, so nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about Carol's job more than mine. If the bookings, invoices and parts ordering all go to software, Dennis might not need her, and that's a family business wobbling. For me, someone's still got to do the work under the car, so I'd be all right for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working, same as always. I'd put more into savings, maybe double what I do now, because if the garage gets tight I want a cushion before the wedding. I still wouldn't touch the AI stuff unless Dennis made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, but for the garage and the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Dennis did make you use the AI tablet on every job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, I'm not daft, he pays my wages. But I'd check everything it said with my own eyes before I touched the car. The day it tells me to replace a part I know is fine, it goes back in the drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is behind this kind of change, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms and the carmakers, working together, and the politicians who let them. They'd love every car to go to a main dealer where a computer tells a kid what to swap. Small places like Dennis's, where a man knows your truck, are what they're squeezing out.

say: A trade is a trade, and **you can't download** a mechanic.
Josh, the apprentice, should **listen to an engine** instead of staring at a tablet.
think: Carol's **office work** looks more at risk than his own.
Someone still has to **work under the car**, so he feels safe for now.
do: **Double his savings** so there's a cushion before the wedding.
Keep working as normal and avoid AI unless **Dennis insists**.
feel: **Uneasy** for the garage and the town more than for himself.
S1.quote: A trade is a trade and you can't download a mechanic.
fieldNote: He worries first about **Carol's desk work**, which is the thinking side of the garage.
He'd use the tablet only under orders and **check every answer** himself.
He blames **tech firms and carmakers**, plus politicians, for squeezing small garages.

steps.text: Double the monthly savings transfer before the wedding
Keep doing jobs by ear and use the tablet only if Dennis says

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I don't believe it, but go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say it's rubbish, and that no robot is getting under a muddy pickup on a farm track. I'd say it at work, at church, anywhere. People round here would mostly agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, if it really happened, the robot bit is what gets me. Three years after 2028 is 2031, I'd be 32, and I've never done anything but this. I don't use any of this AI stuff, so I'd be starting from nothing while the young ones are already ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd move the wedding forward and make it smaller, so it's done before things get bad. I'd throw everything spare at the mortgage, because a paid-off house is the one thing a robot can't take. And I'd ask Dennis straight out what he plans, because I'd rather hear it from him than find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Sick in the stomach. It's not a feeling I'm used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move the wedding forward. How would Chiara take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset about the big day, she's been planning it with her mum for a year. But she's sensible, and her job with the little ones feels safer than mine. We'd keep the church and cut the hotel, and that saves a fair bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the AI tools, given two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep saying no, and I'd probably still say no in public. Privately, I'd maybe get Josh to show me the tablet properly, after hours, so nobody sees me fumbling. But I don't see what learning it does if the robots are coming anyway.

say: It's rubbish, and **no robot** is getting under a muddy pickup on a farm track.
He'd say it at **work and church**, where most people would agree.
think: Robots arriving in **2031** would hit him at 32 with only one trade.
He's never used AI, so he'd be **starting from nothing** behind younger workers.
do: Move the **wedding forward**, keeping the church but cutting the hotel.
Put everything spare into **paying off** the house.
Ask Dennis **straight out** about his plans for the garage.
feel: **Alarmed** and sick in the stomach, a feeling he isn't used to.
S2.quote: A paid-off house is the one thing a robot can't take.
fieldNote: His public dismissal and private **fear** are far apart in this picture.
He sees a **paid-off house** as the one safe thing against robots.
He might secretly let Josh teach him the **tablet after hours**, but doubts the point.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward, keep St Anne's church and drop the hotel
Put every spare bit of pay into clearing the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say people want a person they trust fixing their car, and I'd believe that more with five years than two. At work I'd tell Dennis we should be the garage that keeps the old trucks going, the ones the robots won't bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five plus three is 2034, so I'd be 35. That's a long time to keep earning and pay off the house, but I'd still be out of a trade at 35 with nothing else. I'd hate it, but I'd have to think about something like a foreman's job, where people still want someone in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned next September, no rush. I'd overpay the mortgage every month with the aim of clearing it by 2033. And I'd ask Dennis if there's a way I could buy into the garage over time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sick than the two-year one, but it sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into the garage is a big step for someone who avoids risk. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's bricks and a name in town, not a gamble on some new thing. Dennis is sixty-four and his son went into banking, so somebody has to take it on. I'd rather own my boss's garage myself than watch a chain put robots in the bays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Chiara about the future in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be all right if we keep our heads and don't spend daft. That we'd still have kids, maybe a year or two later than we said. And that I'd sort it, because that's my job.

say: People want a **person they trust** fixing their car.
Dennis's garage should be the one that keeps **old trucks** going.
think: Robots arriving in **2034** would leave him out of a trade at 35.
He'd consider a **foreman's job**, where people still want someone in charge.
do: Keep the **wedding** as planned for next September.
**Overpay the mortgage** monthly to clear it by 2033.
Ask Dennis about **buying into** the garage over time.
feel: **Anxious**, but less sick than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: I'd rather own my boss's garage myself than watch a chain put robots in the bays.
fieldNote: Five years turns him from shock to **planning**, though on familiar ground.
Buying the garage feels safe to him because it's **bricks and a name**, not new tech.
He sees providing for his fiancée Chiara as **his job**, and pushes kids back a year or two.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage every month to clear it by 2033
Ask Dennis Hale to sell him a share of the garage over time
Push back having children by a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 when it arrives. Robots at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lifetime in this trade, and half of it will never happen. At church and at the pub I'd tell people not to get wound up by the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough that I don't have to change anything this year, and I like that. By 2039 the house is paid and the kids are at school. What bothers me is being 40 and having to start again, but I could do it with a paid-off house behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do nothing new, honestly, just keep working and saving. I'd keep an eye on whether the chain garages in the city start using robots, and if they do, I'd start talking to Dennis about the garage. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. It's far off, but it's there at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half of it will never happen. Which half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots fixing old trucks on a farm, mainly. A computer reading fault codes, fine, it already does. But a machine lying in mud under a pickup in January, I'll believe it when I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own kids, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn a trade, same as me, maybe two trades. Not sit at a desk, because that's where the AI comes first. My dad taught me with his hands, and I'd want that for them.

say: Ten years is **a lifetime** in this trade, and half of it won't happen.
People shouldn't get **wound up** by the news.
think: Ten years means he doesn't have to **change anything** this year, which he likes.
Starting again at **40** worries him, but a **paid-off house** would help.
do: Keep **working and saving** as normal in the first year.
Watch whether **city chains** use robots before talking to Dennis about the garage.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the change sitting far off at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: A machine lying in mud under a pickup in January, I'll believe it when I see it.
fieldNote: Long warning lets him **wait**, which suits his dislike of change.
He doubts robots can do **farm-track repairs** in mud and winter.
He'd steer his future kids toward **trades**, away from desks where AI hits first.

steps.text: Keep working and saving at Dennis Hale's garage as normal
Watch whether city chain garages start using robots before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt, because I'd have no time to get the house paid off or find my feet. What would help is the government backing apprenticeships for grown adults, not handouts, so a mechanic of 32 could learn a new trade on a wage. And making the carmakers open up their software, so a garage like Dennis's can still compete.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens with all this, I'll be at St Anne's on Sunday and so will most of this town. A robot might take my job, but a robot can't take my church or my neighbours.

headlineQuote: A robot might take my job, but a robot can't take my church or my neighbours.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old mechanic at **Dennis Hale's garage**, fixing farm pickups and older diesels.
He trusts **ears and a torch** over the AI tablet, which he leaves to the apprentice.
He's engaged to Chiara and puts the **house and wedding** at the centre of every plan.
In the fast AGI picture his **public dismissal** hides real fear of being 32 with one trade.
With more warning he leans on **paying off the house** and maybe buying into the garage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to clear the mortgage or find his feet.
whatWouldHelp: Government-backed **adult apprenticeships** that pay a wage, not handouts.
Making carmakers **open their software** so small garages can compete.
